# The Pipeline of the Decision: How to Transform Confusion into Mathematic Models and AI

The video travels the path of computational decision, from the ill-defined problem to the evaluation of the model. It deals with solvency, the formalization of the problem, the six dimensions of data quality, the choice of machine learning metrics and the limit between machine decision and human judgment.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on August 19, 2026 (8 min 21 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lhEdMm7qvAU

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## Where the systems fail

The video describes the path of computational decision: leaving a chaotic and unstructured reality until the rigorous evaluation of an algorithm [00:00]. The initial question is why complex systems fail so often, even with large investments [00:21]. The answer: the root of failure is not in programming, but before the first line of code [00:43].

## The Trap of Solutionism

Solving is the rush to build complex solutions before understanding what the real problem is [00:43]. According to the video, failures linked to this error of origin compromise up to 70% of IT initiatives [01:03].

To avoid the trap, it is necessary to separate two spaces [01:46]:

- the scope of the problem: the practical context, stakeholders' pains, restrictions and root causes [02:06];
- the solution space: algorithms, code and technical architecture [02:06].

Mixing the two too soon generates systems that work, but are useless in real life [02:06].

## To formalize the problem

Problem engineering is the bridge between the two spaces [02:27]. The central object is the problem representation artifact [02:48]. Written in a declarative language, the Problem Specification Language, it transforms human intentions and needs into a computational object, which people and machines can read, audit and verify [02:48].

With agentic AI, this phase uses several agents [03:09]:

- the structuring agent translates texts and narratives into an initial ontological graph [03:09];
- the critical agent seeks confirmation biases, logic failures and untested assumptions [03:30].

The result is a note. According to the video, the artifact only follows for development if it reaches 0.85 in the quality index of the formulation of the problem (PFQI) [03:52]. The metric punishes ambiguity: vague terms overturn the note [04:12].

## The six dimensions of data quality

A well-defined problem is no good with bad data [04:12]. To avoid "waste comes in, garbage comes out", the video lists six dimensions [04:33]:

- completeness: no empty fields [04:33];
- consistency: no conflict between records of different bases [04:33];
- conformity to specified formats [04:33];
- integrity of the relations between the tables [04:33];
- accuracy: how much the data reflect reality [04:53];
- current: if the information is still relevant today [04:53].

When a machine learning model is trained with bad data, it crystallizes base biases [04:53]. This generates high costs and risks of regulation and compliance [05:15].

## Evaluate models

With good data and a validated problem, machine learning metrics judge the model [05:37]. They are divided into three families, according to the objective [05:37]:

- classification: predict the category of something [05:37];
- regression: predict a continuous numerical value [05:37];
- ranking: sort lists by relevance [05:37].

In the classification, only the accuracy deceives when the data are unbalanced, because it hides faults behind a high percentage [05:59]. The F1 score corrects this with the harmonic mean between precision and recall [06:20].

In regression, the choice between the mean quadratic error (MSE) and the average absolute error (MAE) depends on the impact of the error on the business [06:20]. The MSE raises the error squared and punishes the big mistakes a lot. The MAE treats all errors linearly [06:43]. The choice shall reflect the risk aversion of the organisation [06:43].

## The border between person and machine

AI agents and large language models work by statistical approximation [07:05]. As best the answers are, they do not replace human judgment in moral choices and ethical limits [07:26]. Having a person to validate the final decision is mandatory [07:26].

The final question: if a system calculates everything perfectly, but does not respond legally and socially by the consequences, whose decision is it [07:47]? For the video, strategy, commitments and conscience remain human responsibility [07:47].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is solucionism?

It is the rush to build a complex solution before understanding the real problem [00:43].

### Why use the F1 score instead of accuracy?

Because with unbalanced data, accuracy hides flaws. The F1 score combines precision and recall [06:20].

### When do you prefer MSE or MAE?

Depends on the impact of the error: the MSE punishes the major errors more, and the MAE treats all errors linearly [06:43].

## About the video

Have you ever felt that your team built the perfect solution to the wrong problem? This classic error, known as solvingeering, is what Problem Engineering came to solve.
In this video, we dive into the Pipeline of Decision, a systematic and rigorous process that transforms real ambiguous and "confusive" situations into first-class computer artifacts, ready to be solved by optimization algorithms or artificial intelligence agents.
What you will learn in this video:
The Bridge Between Worlds: How to get out of natural language (intrinsically ambiguous) to the PSL (Problem Specification Language), a formal syntax that computers understand.
The Life Cycle of Formulation: Learn about the four essential macrophases:
Exploration: Discovery and Framework (Framing) to define the boundaries of what will be resolved.
Formalization: Objective Engineering and Structure, where narratives become the Problem Graph (GP).
Verification: The critical phase of multidimensional validation (Semantics, Structural, Empirical, Decision-making and by Stakeholders).
Interface: Safe handover to Solution Space.
The PFQI Index: Learn how to measure the quality of a problem before spending a penny on the solution. We explain the dimensions of Completeness, Logic Consistency, Traceability and the dreaded Penalty for Ambiguity.
Genetic Architecture: How a multi-agent ecosystem (with roles such as Structurer and the Devil's Critic/Advocacy) can accelerate modeling and identify confirmation biases before they cause harm.
Who's this video for?
Data Engineers and Decision Scientists.
Complex Project Managers and Requirements Engineers.
IA developers interested in agentic AI and Governance.
Technical Highlight: The central object of Problem Engineering is not gross empirical reality, but AR P (Problem Representation Artefact) — an ontological, versionable and auditable substrate that serves as the only stable benchmark to evaluate any solution technology.
